overview.summary: Marine biologists study life in the oceans and other salt water, from tiny plankton to whales, and the ecosystems they live in.
overview.problems: They help understand and protect ocean life, fisheries and coasts, and study how oceans are changing.
overview.worksWith: Other scientists, divers and boat crews, fisheries and conservation groups, government agencies and local communities.
overview.workplaces: Research vessels, coastal stations, aquariums, laboratories, universities and conservation organizations.

timeline.title: Preparing fieldwork
timeline.description: The biologist checks the weather, equipment and safety plans.

timeline.title: At sea or on the shore
timeline.description: The biologist collects samples, surveys species or monitors habitats, sometimes by diving or from a boat.
timeline.why: Direct observation gives data you cannot get elsewhere.

timeline.title: Processing samples
timeline.description: The biologist identifies and counts species in the laboratory.
timeline.why: Careful identification is the base of any study.

timeline.title: Data analysis
timeline.description: The biologist uses statistics and software to study patterns.
timeline.why: Patterns show whether populations are healthy.

timeline.title: Writing and communicating
timeline.description: The biologist writes reports and talks to communities and managers.
timeline.why: Findings only protect the ocean when people act on them.

timeline.title: Weather and long trips
timeline.description: Bad weather can cancel plans, and research cruises can last weeks.
timeline.why: Work at sea depends on conditions.

responsibilities: Collecting and analyzing samples and data
Following safety rules for boats and diving
challenges: Jobs are competitive and often short-term or grant-funded.
Fieldwork can be physically demanding and depends on the weather.
Seasickness and time away from home on research trips can be hard.
There are safety risks at sea and in diving.
Much of the time goes on data and writing.
Many roles need a master's degree or PhD.
workEnvironment: A mix of boats, shores, laboratories and offices. Fieldwork can be on research vessels or at coastal sites, in all weather. Office and laboratory work includes analysis and reports.
tradeoffs: Pay that varies by country and employer

activity.title: Build an ocean food web
steps: Choose an ocean habitat such as a kelp forest or a coral reef.
Using trusted sources such as a public aquarium or marine science website, list eight species that live there.
Draw arrows from each food to the animal that eats it, making a web.
Pick one species and write what would happen if it disappeared.
Note whether thinking about connections felt interesting.
activity.outcome: You practise researching, linking facts and thinking about how ecosystems depend on each other.
activity.safety: This is a desk exercise. If you visit a beach, go with an adult, watch tides and waves, never go out alone, and do not touch or remove living animals.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
